reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A slowly progressive chronic tubulointerstitial disease occurring in rural populations along tributaries of the Danube in the Balkan region
It is now widely attributed to chronic dietary exposure to aristolochic acid, a nephrotoxin derived from Aristolochia plants that can contaminate local grain
The same toxin links it mechanistically to aristolochic acid nephropathy seen elsewhere, including cases from certain herbal preparations
It characteristically presents with insidious progressive kidney failure, low-grade tubular proteinuria, small shrunken kidneys, and relatively bland urine
A strong and characteristic association exists with urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the upper urinary tract
Familial clustering within affected villages reflects shared environmental exposure rather than direct inheritance
Management is supportive, centred on slowing progression, avoiding further nephrotoxin exposure, and vigilant surveillance for urothelial malignancy
Aristolochic acid produces a distinctive mutational signature that helps confirm its causative role
reference.pathophysiology: Balkan endemic nephropathy is a chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis driven by long-term ingestion of aristolochic acid, which contaminates food when Aristolochia seeds mingle with wheat in endemic areas. Aristolochic acid and its metabolites form DNA adducts and are directly toxic to renal tubular cells, producing progressive interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and loss of nephrons with characteristically small kidneys. The same DNA-damaging effect, particularly mutations in tumour suppressor genes such as TP53, underlies the strong predisposition to upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma. Individual susceptibility likely reflects genetic differences in toxin metabolism.
additionalDifferentials: Other forms of chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis
Chronic lead or other heavy-metal nephropathy
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of kidney function and progression over time
Urinalysis and quantification of low-grade tubular proteinuria
Renal imaging showing small, shrunken kidneys
Surveillance imaging and urine cytology for upper tract urothelial carcinoma
Exposure history to aristolochic acid-containing plants or herbal remedies
redFlags: Haematuria or imaging findings suggesting upper urinary tract urothelial cancer
New symptoms after use of unregulated herbal products
Multiple affected individuals from the same endemic locality
reference.prognosis: The disease progresses gradually to kidney failure over years, and the markedly increased lifelong risk of urothelial carcinoma is a major determinant of outcome, making cancer surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Failing to consider a toxic (aristolochic acid) aetiology in endemic or herbal-exposure settings
Overlooking the high risk of upper tract urothelial cancer and omitting surveillance
Attributing the disease to inheritance rather than shared environmental exposure
Missing continued exposure to contaminated food or herbal products
